The learning desk

A few useful words.
A clearer way in.

You do not need to know every term to start. These eight building blocks help connect a central bank decision to the market conversation around it.

Concept 01

Policy rate

The interest rate a central bank sets or targets to influence borrowing conditions across the economy. Changes can reach consumers, companies and markets through several channels.

In practice: A rate cut may lower financing costs, but its effect depends on why rates were cut and what markets expected.

Concept 02

Inflation

A broad rise in the prices of goods and services over time. A lower inflation rate usually means prices are rising more slowly, rather than falling.

In practice: If inflation falls from 4% to 2%, the general price level can still be increasing.

Concept 03

Equity index

A measure tracking a defined group of company shares. Its performance depends on which companies it contains and how much weight each company receives.

In practice: A capitalisation-weighted index can rise even when many smaller constituents fall.

Concept 04

Earnings per share (EPS)

A company’s profit allocated to each share. It is one measure investors use when thinking about profitability and valuation.

In practice: If expected profits weaken, a lower interest rate may not be enough to support share prices.

Concept 05

Valuation

The price investors pay relative to a business measure such as earnings, sales or cash flow. A valuation ratio is context, not proof that an investment is cheap or expensive.

In practice: A price-to-earnings ratio compares a share price with earnings per share. Expectations affect how people interpret it.

Concept 06

Discount rate

The rate used to translate future cash flows into a value today. A higher discount rate reduces the present value of the same future cash flows.

In practice: All else equal, a lower discount rate can support a higher present value. In reality, future cash-flow expectations also change.

Concept 07

Policy divergence

A situation in which central banks follow different policy paths because their economies, inflation conditions or assessments differ.

In practice: The historical pilot compares the ECB’s June 2024 cut with the Fed’s decision to hold in the same month.

Concept 08

Priced in

The idea that market prices already reflect some expectations about future events. An event’s impact depends partly on how it differs from those expectations.

In practice: A widely expected rate cut may move markets less than an unexpected change in the central bank’s outlook.

Definitions simplify complex ideas for educational use. Relationships described as “all else equal” are not predictions. No concept on this page is personal investment advice.

Put it together

One question.
Two useful lenses.

Switch the language and keep the same underlying idea.

A rate cut is a clue.
It is not a buy signal.

Lower rates can make borrowing cheaper. But if a central bank is cutting because growth is weakening, company profits may come under pressure. Ask why the rate changed before deciding what it means for equities.

WHY THE CUT?→COSTS + PROFITS→EQUITIES

An educational mechanism, not a forecast. Market expectations matter too.

Policy easing ≠ an automatic equity tailwind.

A lower discount rate can support valuations, but weaker earnings expectations may offset that effect. The equity response depends on the growth backdrop, the policy surprise and what is already priced in.

POLICY RATIONALE→RATES + EPS→VALUATION

EPS means earnings per share. See the glossary for the building blocks.
